common_name: Mocha Moon Hardy Hibiscus (White Red-Eyed Rose Mallow with Bronze Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Mocha Moon dies back completely each winter and is slow to re-emerge, so mark its location and avoid disturbing the crown in early spring.

directions: Mocha Moon bears huge, slightly cupped, pure white flowers 7-8 inches across with a vivid scarlet-red eye that bleeds outward along the petal veins, set off by bright lime-green calyxes and deep bronze-green, dissected foliage. The sizable, well-branched clump blooms continuously from midsummer into fall and is a bred-up sibling of 'Crown Jewels' and 'Midnight Marvel.' Grow in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, and cut the dead canes to the ground in late winter, expecting new growth to emerge later than most perennials.

common_name: Dark Mystery Hardy Hibiscus (Near-Black-Leaved White Red-Eyed Rose Mallow)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Dark Mystery is grown for foliage nearly as dark as its name, among the darkest wine-purple leaf color in hardy hibiscus, contrasting with large white flowers.

directions: Dark Mystery holds some of the darkest foliage of any hardy hibiscus, a rich wine-purple with a chocolatey cast, which it keeps strongly colored through the season rather than fading to green. Against this backdrop open massive, ruffled, 8-9-inch white flowers with a prominent cherry-red eye and fine dark-pink veining radiating into the petals. The vigorous, well-branched clump flowers from midsummer into fall and needs consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun. Cut the dead canes to the ground in late winter, since like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely and emerges late in spring.

common_name: Berrylicious Hardy Hibiscus (Mauve-Lavender Raspberry-Eyed Rose Mallow)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Berrylicious forms a naturally compact, heavily branched mound and has shown good resistance to leaf-spot fungus in trials.

directions: Berrylicious produces ruffled, mauve-lavender flowers with a dark raspberry eye held above medium-green foliage on a naturally compact, densely branched plant that needs less staking than many large-flowered hardy hibiscus. It has shown better-than-average resistance to leaf-spot fungus and some tolerance of deer browsing in trial plantings. Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, where it flowers from midsummer into fall. Cut the dead stems to the ground in late winter and be patient in spring, since it emerges later than most other perennials.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden hardy hibiscus plant evaluation

common_name: Sultry Kiss Hardy Hibiscus (Magenta-Red Giant-Flowered Rose Mallow)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Sultry Kiss forms an upright mound of maple-like foliage that emerges bronze before maturing to dark green.

directions: Deep red buds on Sultry Kiss open to enormous, 9-11-inch magenta-red flowers whose heavily overlapping petals crowd the reddish-purple stems from node to node, coating the plant in bloom from midsummer until frost. The dark green, maple-like foliage emerges bronze in spring before settling into its mature color on an upright, well-branched mound. Grow in consistently moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, where mature plants tolerate brief drought but perform best with steady moisture. Cut the dead canes to the ground in late winter, since the plant dies back fully and is slow to resprout in spring.

common_name: Stardust Hardy Hibiscus (Zone-4-Hardy Speckled Pink Rose Mallow)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Stardust was selected for extreme cold hardiness, performing reliably into USDA zone 4, and forms a compact, rounded clump.

directions: Stardust carries giant, thick-textured flowers 10-11 inches across in red and pink tones, heavily streaked and speckled around a red eye with buttery-yellow anthers. Bronze-tinted, maple-shaped foliage covers a sturdy, rounded, more compact habit than many large-flowered hardy hibiscus. Bred by David Fleming and selected out of a long-running breeding program for outstanding cold tolerance, it performs reliably even in USDA zone 4 gardens where some hardy hibiscus cultivars struggle. Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, and cut the dead canes to the ground in late winter ahead of late-emerging spring growth.

common_name: My Valentine Hardy Hibiscus (Velvety Red Rose Mallow with Burgundy Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; My Valentine is a Summerific-series selection prized as one of the richest true reds among hardy hibiscus.

directions: Deep reddish-black buds on My Valentine open to large, 8-9-inch velvety red flowers with overlapping petals and deep veining around a central pistil tipped in light beige anthers. The three-lobed, deep-green leaves flush burgundy-red on sun-exposed growth through summer and turn amber and gold in autumn. Flowering runs from August into fall on an upright, well-branched plant that is a Summerific-series sibling of 'Valentine's Crush.' Grow in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, cutting the dead stems to the ground in late winter.

common_name: Bleu Brulee Hardy Hibiscus (Blue-Flowered Summer Spice Rose Mallow)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moderately fertile, medium-moisture soil in full to part sun; Bleu Brulee was bred at Texas A&M AgriLife as part of the compact Summer Spice series and was the first hardy hibiscus marketed with blue-toned flowers.

directions: Bleu Brulee opens 8-inch flowers in an unusual lilac-blue to steel-blue tone with a red eye, with the blue cast reading most vividly in morning and evening light and shifting toward lilac-pink under strong midday sun. Narrow, dissected leaves cover a compact, upright plant that concentrates its blooms toward the upper growth, flowering continuously from July into September. Bred at Texas A&M AgriLife's research program as part of the compact Summer Spice series, it was introduced as the first perennial hibiscus marketed with blue flower color. Plant in full to part sun in moderately fertile, medium-moisture soil, where it draws hummingbirds and butterflies while resisting deer and rabbits.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research hardy hibiscus breeding program
J. Berry Nursery Summer Spice series introduction

common_name: Tie Dye Hardy Hibiscus (Dark Pink and White Bull's-Eye Rose Mallow)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Tie Dye produces flat-faced, ruffled flowers in a distinctive bull's-eye pattern on an upright, well-branched plant.

directions: Tie Dye bears flat-faced, deeply ruffled flowers patterned in a bold bull's-eye: a dark-pink outer ring fades to white toward the center, surrounding a lustrous cherry-red eye. The mostly three-lobed, medium-to-dark-green foliage carries only light purple tinting, letting the bicolor blooms stand out, and the strong, upright stems are well branched and self-supporting. It flowers from midsummer into fall and prefers consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun. Cut the dead canes to the ground in late winter, since the plant dies back completely each year and re-emerges later than most perennials.
